title: SQL Basics
text:
SQL Basics

SELECT: Choose your columns.
FROM: Choose your table.
WHERE: Filter individual rows.
GROUP BY: Bundle rows into categories.
HAVING: Filter the bundles/groups.
ORDER BY: Sort your final list.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The SELECT Statement
The SELECT statement is used to pick the columns you want to see.

Basic Syntax:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name;
The Wildcard (Selects all columns):

SELECT * 
  FROM table_name;

The SELECT statement is the most common command. The asterisk is a wildcard, meaning “give me everything,” though it is often better practice to name columns specifically.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The DISTINCT Keyword
Sometimes a column contains many duplicate values. To see only unique values, use DISTINCT.

Syntax:
SELECT DISTINCT column_name 
FROM table_name;
Example:

SELECT DISTINCT country 
    FROM customers;

DISTINCT is incredibly useful for seeing the unique categories or values within a specific column, like a list of countries where your customers live.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 1
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Display the FirstName, LastName, and Email of every customer.
Display each country represented in the Customer table only once.
Display the Name, Composer, and UnitPrice of every track.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Filtering with WHERE
The WHERE clause is used to filter records based on specific conditions.

It acts as a gatekeeper.
If a row doesn’t meet the condition, it is excluded from the results.

Example:
SELECT * 
    FROM products 
    WHERE price > 50;

The WHERE clause is our primary tool for filtering. It allows us to isolate exactly the rows we need from a massive dataset.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Comparison Operators
Use these to compare values in your WHERE clause:

= (Equal to)
!= (Not equal to)
> (Greater than)
< (Less than)
>= (Greater than or equal to)
<= (Less than or equal to)


These operators are the foundation of logical comparisons in SQL.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Logical Operators
You can combine multiple conditions using logic:

AND: Both conditions must be true.
OR: At least one condition must be true.
NOT: The condition must be false.

Example:
SELECT * 
    FROM users 
    WHERE age < 18 AND country = 'USA';

Logical operators allow for complex filtering. AND narrows your results, while OR expands them.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 2
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Find the tracks that cost at least $1.00. Display Name and UnitPrice.
Find customers who live in either the USA or Canada. Display their name and country.
Find invoices from the USA with a total greater than $10.00.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Sorting with ORDER BY
The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set.

Default: Ascending (A-Z, 1-10).
ASC: Explicitly for Ascending.
DESC: Explicitly for Descending (Z-A, 10-1).

Example:
SELECT name, salary 
    FROM employees 
    ORDER BY salary DESC;

Ordering helps us make sense of data by presenting it in a meaningful sequence, like highest salary to lowest.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Sorting Multiple Columns
You can sort by more than one column.

SQL sorts by the first column listed.
If there is a “tie” in the first column, it uses the second column.

Example:
SELECT last_name, first_name 
    FROM employees 
    ORDER BY last_name ASC, first_name ASC;

Sorting by multiple columns is very common when dealing with data that has many duplicate values in the primary sorting column.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 3
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

List customers by Country, then by LastName, and then by FirstName, all in ascending order.
List tracks from highest to lowest UnitPrice. For tracks with the same price, sort by Name in ascending order.
List invoices from highest to lowest Total.


Ask students which column controls the primary sort and which columns break ties.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Aggregation: The Big Idea
Aggregation is the process of performing a calculation on a set of values to return a single value.

Instead of seeing 1,000 individual sales, we want to see the Total Sales.
Aggregation “collapses” rows into summary statistics.


Aggregation turns “row-level” data into “summary-level” data. This is where data becomes “information.”

title: SQL Basics
text:
Common Aggregate Functions

COUNT(): Returns the number of rows.
SUM(): Returns the total sum of a numeric column.
AVG(): Returns the average value.
MIN(): Returns the smallest value.
MAX(): Returns the largest value.


These are the heavy lifters of data analysis. COUNT and SUM are perhaps the most frequently used in business reporting.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The GROUP BY Clause
When using aggregate functions, we often want to see the summary per category.

GROUP BY tells the database how to bucket the data.

Example:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) 
    FROM employees 
    GROUP BY department;

If you use an aggregate function and a regular column together, you MUST use a GROUP BY clause on that regular column.

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 4
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Count the number of tracks in each GenreId.
For each BillingCountry, calculate the number of invoices and the total amount invoiced.
For each AlbumId, calculate the average track length in milliseconds.


Remind students that every selected column that is not inside an aggregate function must appear in the GROUP BY clause.

title: SQL Basics
text:
The HAVING Clause
WHERE cannot be used with aggregate functions. For that, we use HAVING.

WHERE: Filters rows before they are grouped.
HAVING: Filters groups after they are aggregated.

Example:
SELECT category, AVG(price) 
    FROM products 
    GROUP BY category 
    HAVING AVG(price) > 20;

This is a common point of confusion. If you want to filter based on a calculation like “Average” or “Sum,” you must use HAVING.

title: SQL Basics
text:
WHERE vs. HAVING








Feature
WHERE
HAVING




Usage
Filters Rows
Filters Groups


Timing
Before Grouping
After Grouping


Aggregates
Cannot use SUM(), AVG()
Used with SUM(), AVG()




A good rule of thumb: If it’s a simple column condition, use WHERE. If it’s a condition on a summary calculation, use HAVING.

title: SQL Basics
text:
SQL Order of Execution
SQL is not read from top to bottom by the database engine. It follows a specific internal order:

FROM (Pick the table)
WHERE (Filter the rows)
GROUP BY (Group the rows)
HAVING (Filter the groups)
SELECT (Pick columns)
ORDER BY (Sort results)


Understanding this is the “secret sauce” to debugging complex queries. If your code is failing, it’s likely because you’re trying to use a column in the WHERE clause that hasn’t been selected yet!

title: SQL Basics
text:
ACTIVITY 5
Use the Chinook database to answer the following questions:

Find billing countries whose total invoiced amount is greater than $100.
Find genres that contain more than 100 tracks. Use GenreId to identify each genre.
Find billing countries whose average invoice total is greater than $6.00.


Have students first write each grouped query without HAVING, then add the condition that filters the aggregated results.

SQL Basics

Activity 2 Solutions
-- 1. Tracks that cost at least $1.00
SELECT Name, UnitPrice
FROM Track
WHERE UnitPrice >= 1.00;

-- 2. Customers in the USA or Canada
SELECT FirstName, LastName, Country
FROM Customer
WHERE Country = 'USA' OR Country = 'Canada';

-- 3. USA invoices greater than $10.00

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 3 Solutions
-- 1. Customers sorted by country and name
SELECT FirstName, LastName, Country
FROM Customer
ORDER BY Country ASC, LastName ASC, FirstName ASC;

-- 2. Tracks sorted by price and then name
SELECT Name, UnitPrice
FROM Track
ORDER BY UnitPrice DESC, Name ASC;

-- 3. Invoices sorted from highest to lowest total
SELECT InvoiceId, CustomerId, Total
FROM Invoice

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 4 Solutions
-- 1. Number of tracks in each genre
SELECT GenreId, COUNT(*) AS TrackCount
FROM Track
GROUP BY GenreId;

-- 2. Invoice count and total amount by country
SELECT BillingCountry,
       COUNT(*) AS InvoiceCount,
       SUM(Total) AS TotalInvoiced
FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry;

-- 3. Average track length for each album
SELECT AlbumId, AVG(Milliseconds) AS AverageMilliseconds
FROM Track
GROUP BY AlbumId;

title: SQL Basics
text:
Activity 5 Solutions
-- 1. Countries with more than $100 in invoice totals
SELECT BillingCountry, SUM(Total) AS TotalInvoiced
FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry
HAVING SUM(Total) > 100;

-- 2. Genres with more than 100 tracks
SELECT GenreId, COUNT(*) AS TrackCount
FROM Track
GROUP BY GenreId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;

-- 3. Countries with an average invoice total over $6.00
SELECT BillingCountry, AVG(Total) AS AverageInvoiceTotal
FROM Invoice
GROUP BY BillingCountry
HAVING AVG(Total) > 6.00;

title: Data Modeling
text:
Data Modeling
Data modeling is the process of describing how data is organized, connected, and constrained before building a database.

Welcome students and frame data modeling as the planning step before implementation. Emphasize that a good model reduces confusion, duplication, and future redesign.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Why Data Modeling Matters
A data model helps teams agree on:

What data must be stored
How different concepts relate
Which rules protect data quality
How the database supports real questions


Ask students to imagine building a database without a plan. Use examples like duplicate customer records, missing orders, or unclear relationships between students and courses.

title: Data Modeling
text:
From Real World to Database
Data modeling translates real-world objects and processes into database structures.

Explain that models become more detailed over time. Conceptual models focus on ideas, logical models focus on structure, and physical models focus on implementation details.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Three Levels of Data Models








Level
Main question
Typical output




Conceptual
What does the organization need to track?
Entities and relationships


Logical
How should the data be structured?
Tables, columns, keys, and constraints


Physical
How will the DBMS store and access it?
Data types, indexes, and storage choices




Use this slide to separate planning from implementation. Students often jump straight to tables, but conceptual thinking helps them understand the domain first.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entity-Relationship Diagrams
An Entity-Relationship diagram, or ER diagram, visually represents:

Entities
Attributes
Relationships
Cardinality rules


Define ER diagrams as a communication tool. They help non-programmers and technical users discuss the structure of a database before creating tables.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Entities
An entity is a thing about which we want to store data.
Examples:

Student
Course
Instructor
Enrollment
Product
Order


Emphasize that entities often become tables in a relational database. Ask students to name entities from a familiar system such as a library, store, or university.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Attributes
An attribute is a fact or property stored about an entity.
For a Student entity, attributes might include:

student_id
first_name
last_name
email
major


Point out that attributes often become columns. Encourage students to distinguish attributes from entities. For example, a student’s name is usually an attribute, while student is the entity.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Identify Entities and Attributes
Scenario: A college wants to track students, courses, instructors, departments, and course enrollments.
Time: 8 minutes
Deliverable: A labeled list containing:

At least 3 entities
At least 2 attributes per entity


Give students 8 to 10 minutes. Walk around and check whether they are mixing up entities and attributes. Bring the class back by asking for one example entity and its attributes.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Relationships
A relationship describes how entities are connected.
Examples:

A student enrolls in a course
An instructor teaches a course
A department offers many courses
An order contains products


Explain that relationships are usually verbs or actions connecting nouns. Encourage students to write relationships as short sentences.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Cardinality
Cardinality describes how many records can participate in a relationship.
Common types:

One-to-one
One-to-many
Many-to-many


Introduce cardinality as the rules of participation. Use practical wording: one student can enroll in many courses; one course can have many students.

title: Data Modeling
Data Modeling
Data Modeling
text:
Many-to-Many Relationship
A many-to-many relationship means many records in Entity A can connect to many records in Entity B.
Example:

Many students can enroll in many courses
Many products can appear in many orders


Explain that many-to-many relationships cannot usually be implemented directly as two tables in a relational database. They need an associative table.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Draw Cardinality
For each statement, decide the cardinality:

A department has many instructors.
A student has one university ID card.
A student enrolls in many courses, and a course has many students.
A customer places many orders.

Then sketch a simple ER diagram for each. Label each relationship with a verb.

Give students 10 minutes. Encourage them to label relationships clearly. Afterward, review each statement and ask students how they knew the cardinality.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Resolving Many-to-Many Relationships
Many-to-many relationships are usually resolved with a bridge table, also called an associative table.

Explain that Enrollment stores the connection between a student and a course. It can also store relationship-specific attributes such as enrollment date or grade.

Keys in Relational Databases
Keys help identify records and connect tables.








Key type
Purpose
Example




Primary key
Uniquely identifies a row
student_id in Student


Foreign key
References a row in another table
student_id in Enrollment


Composite key
Uses multiple columns for uniqueness
(student_id, course_id, term)


Candidate key
Could serve as the primary key
A verified, unique email address




Transition from diagrams to implementation. Explain that keys are what make relationships enforceable in a relational database.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Primary Keys
A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.
A good primary key should be:

Unique
Not missing
Stable over time
Simple to reference


Explain that primary keys prevent ambiguity. Mention that IDs are often used because names and emails can change or repeat.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Foreign Keys
A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key in another table.
Foreign keys are used to:

Connect related tables
Enforce valid relationships
Prevent orphan records


Use the phrase parent table and child table if helpful. Explain that a foreign key makes sure a course references a real department or an enrollment references a real student.

Primary and Foreign Keys Together

Point out that the same value can be a primary key in one table and a foreign key in another. The role depends on the table where the column appears.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Activity: Find the Keys
Given these tables, identify the primary keys and foreign keys.
Student(student_id, first_name, last_name)
Course(course_id, course_name, department_id)
Enrollment(enrollment_id, student_id, course_id, enrolled_on)
Questions:

Which fields uniquely identify rows?
Which fields connect tables?
Which table resolves a many-to-many relationship?


Give students 8 minutes. Ask them to mark primary keys with PK and foreign keys with FK. Review that Enrollment connects Student and Course.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Composite Keys
A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.
Example:
Enrollment(student_id, course_id, term)
Together, these fields can identify one student’s enrollment in one course during one term.

Explain that composite keys are useful when no single field is enough. Also mention that some designers still add a separate enrollment_id for convenience.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Why Normalize Data?
Normalization stores each fact in the table where it belongs.








Problem
Example
Risk




Repeated data
A customer’s name appears on every order line
Updates can disagree


Insert anomaly
A product cannot be recorded until someone orders it
Valid facts cannot be stored


Delete anomaly
Deleting the final order removes the only product record
Valid facts disappear




Connect each anomaly to a business consequence. A normalized design reduces these risks by storing customer facts once, product facts once, and transactions separately.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Normal Forms at a Glance








Normal form
Requirement
Question to ask




1NF
Atomic values and no repeating groups
Does each cell contain one value?


2NF
1NF plus no partial dependencies
Does each non-key field depend on the whole key?


3NF
2NF plus no transitive dependencies
Does a non-key field depend on another non-key field?




Emphasize that normalization is cumulative. A table must satisfy 1NF before it can satisfy 2NF, and it must satisfy 2NF before it can satisfy 3NF.

title: Data Modeling
text:
First Normal Form
A table satisfies first normal form when:

Each cell contains one value
Each column describes one type of fact
Each row has a unique identifier
Repeating column groups do not appear

title: Data Modeling
text:
Dependencies in the 1NF Table
order_id                  -> order_date, customer_id
customer_id               -> customer_name
product_id                -> product_name, unit_price
(order_id, product_id)    -> quantity
quantity depends on the complete key. Several other fields depend on only part of the key.

Read each line as “determines.” One order_id determines its date and customer. One product_id determines its name and current unit price. The full order-product key determines quantity.

title: Data Modeling
text:
Partial Dependencies in the 1NF Table
The key is (order_id, product_id).

order_date, customer_id, and customer_name depend on order_id
product_name and unit_price depend on product_id

title: Data Systems
text:
What is a Data System?
A data system is a collection of interconnected components used to collect, store, process, and analyze data.

Input: Raw data (logs, transactions, sensor readings).
Process: Transformation and cleaning.
Storage: Databases or Data Lakes.
Output: Insights, reports, or machine learning models.


Think of a data system like a water treatment plant. You have raw water (input), a filtration system (processing), a reservoir (storage), and tap water for consumption (output).

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Types: The Big Picture
Data is categorized based on how much “organization” it has before it enters a system.

Structured: Highly organized (e.g., Excel, SQL).
Semi-structured: Organized but flexible (e.g., JSON, XML).
Unstructured: No predefined model (e.g., Video, PDF, Audio).


Understanding the format of your data determines what kind of database you need and how much work you have to do to clean it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Structured Data

Tabular (rows and columns).
Highly organized.
Easily searchable.
Examples:

Customer names and addresses.
Transaction amounts and dates.
Inventory counts.



Structured data is the most common form of data handled by traditional businesses. It fits perfectly into spreadsheets and relational databases.

title: Data Systems
text:
Semi-Structured Data

Does not reside in a rigid grid.
Contains tags or markers to separate data elements.
Flexible schema (can change easily).
Examples:

JSON: Used in web APIs.
XML: Used in configuration files.
CSV: Simple comma-separated values.



Semi-structured data is the “middle ground.” It has some hierarchy and markers, but you can add new fields without rebuilding the whole table.

title: Data Systems
Data Systems
text:
Unstructured Data

No internal structure or predefined model.
Makes up the vast majority of data generated today.
Requires specialized tools (AI/ML) to extract meaning.
Examples:

Emails (the text part).
Images and Videos.
Social media posts.



Think of a photo. A computer just sees a bunch of pixels. It doesn’t know it’s a “cat” until an unstructured data processing tool (like an AI model) analyzes it.

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Databases (RDBMS)
The traditional way of storing structured data.

Core Concept: Data is organized into tables.
Schema: Rigid and predefined (must define columns before inserting data).
Relationships: Tables are linked via “Keys” (Primary and Foreign keys).
Example: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle.


In a relational database, if you want to add a “Phone Number” column, you have to update the entire table structure first. This is called a “schema change.”

title: Data Systems
text:
Relational Properties: ACID
To ensure data integrity, RDBMS follow ACID properties:

Atomicity: “All or nothing” transactions.
Consistency: Data follows all rules (no broken links).
Isolation: Transactions don’t interfere with each other.
Durability: Once saved, it stays saved (even if power fails).


ACID is critical for banking. If you transfer $10, the money must leave your account AND arrive in the other account. It cannot do one without the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL)
Designed for modern, high-scale, and flexible data.

Core Concept: Data is stored as documents, key-value pairs, or graphs.
Schema: Dynamic/Flexible (no predefined structure required).
Scalability: Designed to scale “out” (adding more servers).
Example: MongoDB (Document), Redis (Key-Value), Neo4j (Graph).


NoSQL is the response to the “Big Data” explosion. When you have massive amounts of unstructured or semi-structured data, relational databases can struggle to scale.

text:
Activity 2: The Architect’s Dilemma
Scenario: You are building a new social media app like Instagram.
Requirements:

You need to store user profiles (Name, Email, Password).
You need to store millions of high-resolution images.
You need to store a “Follower” graph (who follows whom).

Task: Which database type (Relational or NoSQL) would you use for each requirement? Why?

This is a real-world scenario. Most big apps use a “Hybrid” approach. For example, SQL for user accounts and a NoSQL/Graph database for the social connections.

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipelines
Data doesn’t just sit there; it moves.
Definition: A sequence of data processing steps where a set of data is passed through a series of transformations.
Goal: To move data from a source (where it’s created) to a destination (where it’s used).

A pipeline is like a conveyor belt in a factory. Raw materials go in one end, and finished products come out the other.

title: Data Systems
text:
ETL vs. ELT
The two main ways to move data:


ETL
(Extract, Transform, Load)

Extract from source.
Transform in a staging area (cleaning/filtering).
Load into the target database.


ELT
(Extract, Load, Transform)

Extract from source.
Load directly into the target (Data Lake).
Transform inside the target database using its own power.



ETL was the standard for decades. ELT is becoming more popular because modern cloud warehouses (like Snowflake) are incredibly powerful at processing data once it’s inside.

text:

    Ext --> Trans[Transformation]
    Trans --> Load[Loading/Storage]
    Load --> Anal[Analytics/BI]







This shows the journey from the moment a user clicks a button on a website to the moment a CEO sees a chart on their dashboard. A linear flow: Source \(\rightarrow\) Extraction \(\rightarrow\) Transformation \(\rightarrow\) Loading \(\rightarrow\) Analytics.

title: Data Systems
text:
Data Pipeline Components

Source: Where data originates (App logs, DBs, APIs).
Ingestion: The process of pulling data from the source.
Processing/Transformation: Cleaning, aggregating, or renaming fields.
Storage: The final destination (Data Warehouse or Data Lake).
Orchestration: The “brain” that schedules and monitors the steps.


Orchestration is very important. If the “Extraction” step fails, the “Transformation” step shouldn’t try to run on old or broken data.

CREATE TABLE table_name (

);

text:
SQL command reference: database structure







Keyword or term
Definition




PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
Turns on foreign-key enforcement for the current SQLite connection.


CREATE TABLE
Creates a new table and defines its columns and constraints.


TEXT
Stores text values such as names, identifiers, and grades. (Data Type)



PRAGMA changes a SQLite setting. The other items define the structure of the database.

Explain that TEXT is a data type rather than a command. SQLite must enable foreign-key enforcement separately for each connection, so students should run the PRAGMA statement whenever they reopen the database.

title: Database Building
text:
SQL command reference: constraints







Keyword or clause
Definition




PRIMARY KEY
Uniquely identifies each row in a table.


NOT NULL
Requires the column to contain a value.


UNIQUE
Prevents duplicate values in a column or group of columns.


FOREIGN KEY
Identifies a column whose values must match a key in another table.


REFERENCES
Names the parent table and parent column for a foreign key.


ON DELETE CASCADE
Automatically deletes related child rows when a parent row is deleted.



PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
This composite key prevents a student from enrolling in the same course twice.

Contrast entity integrity, which comes from primary keys, with referential integrity, which comes from foreign keys. Ask students to identify the parent and child table in one relationship.

title: Database Building
text:
SQL command reference: inserting data







Keyword or clause
Definition




INSERT INTO
Adds one or more rows to a table.


VALUES
Introduces the values for the new rows.


NULL
Represents a missing or unknown value when the column permits it.



INSERT INTO majors (major_id, major_name)
VALUES
    ('M01', 'Data Science'),
    ('M02', 'Computer Science');
The value order must match the order of the named columns.

Recommend naming columns in INSERT statements. Doing so makes the statement easier to read and prevents mistakes if the table’s physical column order changes.

title: Database Building
text:
SQL command reference: retrieving data



Keyword or clause
Definition




SELECT
Chooses the columns returned by a query.


FROM
Identifies the first table used by the query.


AS
Assigns a temporary alias to a table or column.


JOIN
Combines matching rows from related tables.


ON
States the condition used to match rows in a join.


ORDER BY
Sorts the result using one or more columns.



FROM students AS s
JOIN majors AS m
    ON s.major_id = m.major_id
The aliases s and m shorten qualified column names.

Explain that an unqualified column name may become ambiguous when several joined tables contain a column with the same name. Aliases make the source of each column explicit.
